title: Bitcoin++ Announces Antarctica Edition For January 2028
text:
bitcoin++ is planning its first cold-storage edition on a 13-day expedition to the Antarctic Peninsula.
Bitcoin developers have gathered all around the world in places like Austin, Berlin, and Florianópolis, to name a few. In early 2028, a group of them plans to meet at the bottom of the world. bitcoin++ has announced Antarctica: Cold Storage Edition, scheduled for January 24 to February 5, 2028. There are only 22 spots available.
The event pairs a technical conference with an expedition ship that departs from Ushuaia, Argentina, crosses the Drake Passage, explores the Antarctic Peninsula, and returns to Ushuaia.
The event plays on bitcoin’s cold storage, the practice of keeping keys offline. The organizers describe the trip as a way to take the conversation somewhere colder, with room for discussions that would otherwise fit into a hallway.
bitcoin++ runs technical conferences, workshops, and hackathons for bitcoin developers. The series began in Austin in 2022 and has since held events in Berlin, Florianópolis, Buenos Aires, Mexico City, Riga, Istanbul, Taipei, Las Vegas, Vienna, Nairobi, Toronto, and Seoul. Each edition carries a theme, from “learn me a bitcoin” in Austin in 2022 to “lightning” in Berlin in 2025.
The organization counts some 20 archived editions. Its next conference, bitcoin++ Seoul, privacy edition, takes place November 5 and 6, 2026.
The trip runs 13 days and 12 nights. The ship leaves Ushuaia on January 24 and crosses the Drake Passage to the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula. Possible stops include Neko Harbour, Paradise Bay, Port Lockroy, and the Lemaire Channel.
According to the trip’s website, activities may include kayaking, camping, hiking, snowshoeing, and Zodiac outings. The organizers note that weather, ice, and expedition decisions determine where the ship lands.
The conference follows an unconference format. Attendees propose the talks, demos, and discussions. The ship will have Starlink and a private room for impromptu hackathons and working sessions.
Reservations are open right now. Fares are quoted in US dollars per person and range from $14,900 in a four-person cabin to $16,700 in a two-person cabin. Passengers may pay in five equal installments or pay in full at signup. Paying the full fare in bitcoin reduces the cost by 5%. The cost of the fare includes parkas.
The final payment is due October 1, 2027. Medical, evacuation, and repatriation insurance is required and purchased separately. Sponsors can place their brands on the expedition parkas. Placements range from $5,000 to $25,000, and each covers about 22 parkas.
The expedition explores the Antarctic Peninsula, not the geographic South Pole.

title: Ripple Secures Final OCC Approval for National Trust Bank
text:
The approval clears the way for Ripple to manage reserves backing its RLUSD stablecoin and provide digital asset custody.
Ripple announced Monday that its national trust bank has secured final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).
The approval completes the chartering process for Ripple National Trust Bank (RNTB), which received conditional approval from the OCC in December 2025.
The federally supervised trust bank is authorized to manage reserves backing Ripple USD (RLUSD), act as collateral trustee for the benefit of RLUSD holders and provide digital asset custody services, according to Ripple.
RLUSD will continue to be issued by Standard Custody & Trust Company, Ripple’s limited purpose trust company regulated by the New York Department of Financial Services.
“We’ve always said crypto and banks work better together — this is what that looks like. Real innovation, real accountability, federal oversight,” Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse said on X on Monday.
Ripple follows Circle, which secured final OCC approval in July. Other crypto firms remain at the conditional approval stage, including Coinbase, which received its preliminary green light in April, and Crypto.com and Stripe-owned Bridge, which received conditional approvals in February.
A national trust bank is a federally chartered institution focused on holding and managing assets on behalf of clients. Unlike a typical commercial bank, most national trust banks do not accept deposits or make loans and do not carry Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insurance, according to the OCC.

Keystone Hackers Steal Key Used to Verify Wallets
text:
Keystone initially disclosed a leak of customer information but has since disclosed that hackers also stole a key that could allow counterfeit wallets to pass authenticity checks.
Hardware wallet maker Keystone said an attacker who breached its website last week also stole a key used to verify the authenticity of its devices, widening the scope of an incident initially disclosed as a customer data leak.
In a statement Monday, Keystone said the stolen authentication key could allow attackers to produce counterfeit wallets that pass its authenticity checks.
“These devices could then be sold or shipped to customers, who might unknowingly use them as genuine products, potentially resulting in asset theft,” Keystone said.
The incident adds to a series of attacks targeting hardware wallet manufacturers this year.
Earlier this month, Ledger asked resellers across Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to suspend sales following reports that devices sold in the region contained unauthorized implants capable of capturing recovery phrases.
In late July, Coldcard manufacturer Coinkite issued a warning to users after attackers exploited a bug that caused its devices to generate wallet seeds with less entropy than intended, resulting in the theft of millions of dollars in crypto.
In its latest update, Keystone said the attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party monitoring tool used by its website to escalate privileges.
“This enabled the attacker to obtain some customer information and a key used to verify the authenticity of our devices.”
Keystone said it plans to destroy 18,835 devices in its inventory that contain the compromised key and has suspended production shipments of all devices using it.
The company said shipments would resume once it begins producing devices with a new authentication key.
Keystone said devices manufactured and delivered before the Oct. 20 incident should be considered safe and that their authenticity checks remain trustworthy.
However, it could not guarantee the authenticity of devices delivered after that date and urged affected customers to contact its support team for additional verification.
Keystone also disclosed the extent of the customer data breach, saying its website’s Shopify store had generated 51,083 buyer records.
Of those, 25,119 had been deleted per its 180-day data retention policy.
However, the remaining 25,964 records dating from 2024 to 2026 were stolen by the attacker. Keystone said the older entries were not deleted due to a failure in its automated tool used to handle bulk erasure of data.
“The tool did not operate reliably. Some erasure tasks failed, and we did not detect and address these failures in time, resulting in certain personal information being retained beyond the permitted period,” Keystone said.
Related: Keystone says website breach exposed hardware wallet buyers’ addresses
In addition, the attacker managed to steal another 12,873 customer checkout records retained by Shopify — information from purchases that had not been completed.
Keystone said it had contacted Shopify to request the deletion of personal information in checkout records retained for more than 30 days.
The incident echoes a June 2020 data breach at Ledger that exposed more than 1 million email addresses, along with customer names, phone numbers and physical addresses. The leaked information fueled years of phishing attempts targeting affected users.
Other hardware wallet manufacturers have also suffered breaches involving customer information and third-party services this year.
In August, Trezor disclosed a breach at its shipping partner that exposed customer information, with the number of affected users expanding to more than 80,000 in September.
SafePal also reported an order-tracking vulnerability in August that exposed data belonging to nearly 40,000 customers, while BitBox was targeted in a September phishing campaign involving a compromised third-party email provider.

StoneX lifts Strive price target 34% as new stock offering bolsters bitcoin strategy
text: StoneX has raised its price target for bitcoin treasury company Strive (ASST) to $43 from $32, citing an improved outlook for the firm's bitcoin (BTC) accumulation strategy. In a Monday research report, StoneX Senior Equity Research Analyst Mark Palmer reiterated a Buy rating on the stock. Strive's ASST shares lost 9.15% to close at $26.32 on Monday, putting the price target 63% above their current prices. On Oct. 20, Strive announced that it raised $630 million in gross proceeds after closing an upsized initial public offering of 7 million shares of its 15% SATS preferred stock. Strive's traditional warrants also expired during the same week, according to its filing. "Taken together, we view the two events as a clean reset of the company's capital structure that underlines its durable, all-preferred bitcoin treasury model," Palmer said. The analyst noted that the company has spent the past year proving that it can finance bitcoin acquisitions entirely with perpetual preferred equity, "with its SATA preferreds doing the heavy lifting." "Now, with the initial public offering of SATS, the company is showing that it can run two preferreds side by side, each built for a different kind of income investor," he added. Stacked Market Caps of Bitcoin Treasury Companies ( The Block ) SATS carries a 15% annual dividend, and the company has set aside enough to cover the first 18 months of payments. SATA, meanwhile, is the firm's earlier variable-rate Series A perpetual preferred stock. Palmer also said that SATA holders should view the introduction of SATS as a positive. "Because SATS sits beneath SATA in terms of priority, every dollar it raises adds assets without adding claims ahead of the senior preferreds," the analyst added. Separately, Strive announced Monday that it purchased 6,182 BTC between Oct. 17 and Oct. 23, bringing its total holdings to 43,000 BTC. That ranked it fourth among public corporate bitcoin holders, according to Bitcointreasuries data.

title: Ripple gets a final go-ahead to launch its own U.S. national trust bank
text:
Ripple, a fintech company building blockchain and crypto for cross-border transactions, and tokenization, can now run a specialized bank under U.S. federal supervision.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the regulator that oversees national banks, has approved Ripple National Trust Bank (RNTB), Ripple’s CEO Brad Garlinghouse announced on X late Monday.
In other words, one of crypto’s biggest players now has a traditional banking-style license, signaling that digital assets are being pulled further into the regulated traditional financial system. Ripple first applied for the banking license in July 2025, and the OCC gave it conditional approval that December before signing off fully this week.
The approval is consistent with Garlinghouse’s long-running pitch that crypto companies should build products that banks and big institutions can actually use.
The RNTB will be tasked with managing the reserves backing Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin. These reserves are essentially real money and assets that provide the token its value.
The bank will also act as a trustee for these reserves and offer regulated custody services, which means it will safely hold digital assets for big companies as they use crypto in payments, trading, and treasury management.
RLUSD will still be issued by Ripple’s New York-regulated unit, Standard Custody & Trust Company. The new bank adds another layer of oversight: RLUSD now has both state and federal regulators watching over parts of its setup.
RLUSD debuted in December 2024 and has since grown to a market value of about $2.5 billion, putting it among the world's top 50 stablecoins. It is used in Ripple’s payments business and as collateral on Ripple Prime. The stablecoin is backed by U.S. dollar deposits, U.S. government securities, and other cash-like assets. BNY holds most of those reserves. Ripple also uses XRP, the world’s 5th largest digital asset, to facilitate cross-border transactions.
Ripple said it will keep working with the OCC, New York regulators, and others as the bank starts operating, especially as the U.S. rolls out its new stablecoin rules under the GENIUS Act.

title: RedotPay Eyes Confidential US IPO Filing by Year-End
text:
The stablecoin payments company previously disputed reports that its US listing had been delayed.
Hong Kong-based stablecoin payments company RedotPay is reportedly considering a confidential filing for a US initial public offering by the end of 2026, two months after reports that it had delayed its listing plans amid regulatory and legal hurdles.
RedotPay is also in talks with investors about a potential pre-IPO funding round that could value the company at between $4 billion and $5 billion, Bloomberg reported Monday, citing people familiar with the matter.
RedotPay says it has more than 8 million users, while data from Paymentscan shows $410.5 million in 30-day stablecoin card transaction volume.
The company was first reported in February exploring a New York listing that could raise more than $1 billion at a valuation exceeding $4 billion, with JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and Jefferies reportedly working on the offering.
However, Bloomberg reported in August that RedotPay had delayed its US listing plans amid regulatory hurdles and legal disputes involving Binance.
The company subsequently disputed that characterization, reportedly saying “there has been no deferral of our IPO,” and that the company is “continuing to work with our partners on the IPO process.”
In August, Binance-affiliated companies sued the founders of RedotPay, seeking nearly $473 million in damages over allegations that they used confidential information to build a competing payments business and divert customers.
RedotPay has denied the allegations and previously told Cointelegraph that it would “vigorously defend all claims.”

title: Zcash co-founder proposes ending grants funding, citing $125 million treasury
text:
Zcash co-founder Sean Bowe has proposed ending automatic funding for the privacy network’s community grants program, saying its treasury is now big enough to cover years of spending without any new money coming in.
His draft proposal, published late Monday, would halt auto allocation and redirect its remaining 8% share of the newly created ZEC into a reserve for future mining rewards.
The committee would keep its existing assets and continue awarding grants from them. Bowe’s calculation puts those assets, after outstanding grant commitments, at about $125 million, using an illustrative ZEC price of $1,300.
It's time to turn off the ZCG funding stream.ZCG has over $125M in funding, and will receive millions more before the spigot is turned off. The program was never designed to handle this amount of funding.Draft ZIP:https://t.co/GAkRBeplwO
ZCG’s five-member committee, elected by a community advisory panel, selects grants without a separate coinholder vote.
A second funding program receives 12% of newly created ZEC. Holders vote quarterly on its grants, subject to participation and approval requirements.
Bowe wants to preserve that larger allocation. His proposal argues that continuing to pile funds into ZCG’s separate custody and governance arrangements adds risk when the program already has substantial reserves.
The redirected allocation would enter the Network Sustainability Mechanism, which is designed to support future mining rewards, and would remain there for the rest of the grants stream’s existing term.
The committee’s dashboard showed about 91,453 ZEC and $8.8 million, with $2.4 million committed to grantees. Bowe values the remaining balance at $125.3 million using a ZEC price of $1,300.
The automatic allocation continues regardless of how much the committee already holds. At the network’s target pace, it receives about 144 ZEC a day, worth about $68 million a year.
For comparison, the Financial Privacy Foundation, which administers ZCG’s funds, reported just over $1.5 million in program expenses for the first quarter. Annualized, that’s about $6 million, less than a tenth of the yearly inflow.
The dollar figures move with ZEC. Even at $500 per coin, Bowe estimates the existing treasury would cover about five years of spending at an assumed $10 million a year.
The proposal arrived amid criticism of a ZCG-funded outreach program that demonstrated private payments at an adult-industry convention over the weekend.
ZECsy, the team behind the program, requested $550,000 for work spanning adult-industry events, crypto conferences and workshops. The pitch included helping workers facing banking restrictions accept payments without exposing personal financial information.
Day 2: Zcash at @EXXXOTICA . @rollergirlVi and @kate_stapes in Mama's zcash kitchen. Giving away protections for your body and your money. Privacy is ZECsy. pic.twitter.com/dkSY3GjhlC
The committee approved startup funding and the first nine milestones, totaling about $461,500. Photos from its Exxxotica booth in Edison, New Jersey, circulated on X on Sunday.
As such, the August approval was split. Committee member Hanh opposed the grant, questioning its cost and evidence of lasting adoption. Other members backed the team’s ability to reach new users, while the nine-month limit allowed an assessment before further funding.
Bowe’s draft does not cite the ZECsy grant, and rests on the program’s reserves and continuing inflows.
The proposal has no activation date and would require a change to Zcash’s network rules. But until one takes effect, ZCG’s allocation continues at about 144 ZEC a day.

ETH news: Ethereum fixes Glamsterdam bug that could have sent staking deposits to builders
text:
Ethereum developers have patched a flaw in the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade that could have let someone walk off with ETH that staking services meant for new validators.
The fix, which changed the rules for handling validator deposits, was merged Monday, a week after developers turned it down.
Glamsterdam splits up two jobs that are bundled together today. Builders put blocks of transactions together, and validators, who stake ETH to help secure the network, pick and confirm them. Both can deposit ETH, and their money is supposed to be tracked separately.
The problem appeared during the upgrade itself, when Ethereum would process deposits that were still waiting to be credited.
Researcher avsetsin identified a scenario in which an operator first registers as a builder using a particular public key, the identifier tied to a validator or builder. If a staking service then deposits ETH to start a validator under that key, the draft rules would credit both deposits to the builder.
“The operator can withdraw the protocol’s funds,” avsetsin wrote. No validator gets created, so the staking service can’t produce the proof it would need to recover its money.
Avsetsin, who is listed as a member of Lido’s GitHub organization, looked at how Lido, Origin and Rocket Pool could be affected, in what the researcher called “quick AI research.” The findings depended on how each protocol handles deposits.
“These are conditional code findings, not confirmed live exploits,” avsetsin wrote, adding that existing checks rejecting an earlier builder deposit could stop the attack. No losses have been reported.
Developers closed the proposed fix on Oct. 19. “There was not enough support from clients to make this change at this time,” wrote Justin Traglia, who maintains Ethereum’s consensus specifications. Clients are the separate software programs validators run to take part in the network.
The fix was reopened after further review, avsetsin added tests on Oct. 23, and Traglia merged it Monday.
Under the new rules, pending deposits are sorted by their withdrawal credentials, the setting that says where a deposit’s money can eventually go. Validator deposits stay with validators even if a builder is using the same key.
The change is now part of Ethereum’s consensus specifications, and client teams still have to build it into their software. Glamsterdam has already run on the Sepolia test network, but its Oct. 26 launch on Hoodi, a second test network, was postponed.
Glamsterdam needs a new Hoodi date before a mainnet launch can be scheduled.

title: SOL news: Solana bug reports now cost 1 SOL as AI floods security teams with spam
text:
A flood of AI-assisted bug reports has prompted the team behind Solana’s Firedancer software to charge researchers 1 SOL, worth about $100, per submission, aiming to cut spam and give engineers more time to investigate genuine security flaws.
The tokens must be burned, which permanently removes them from circulation. Under terms updated Monday, the cost is nonrefundable even if a report is invalid, outside the program’s scope or duplicates an earlier finding. Reports submitted without a burn are ineligible for rewards.
Trading firm Jump Crypto built Firedancer as an alternative to Agave, the main software used by the computers that check and process Solana transactions.
A serious flaw can stop those computers processing payments or make them disagree about account balances, disrupting trades and transfers. Hundreds of duplicate or unworkable reports take engineers’ time away from investigating and fixing those vulnerabilities.
A $1 million audit competition held between April 9 and May 9 attracted 809 reports from 162 researchers. Those produced 127 unique security findings, excluding non-exploitable observations. Nearly half of valid submissions were duplicates.
Jump believes AI agents helped discover or write nearly every submission.
“AI has made finding bugs cheap, but judging them is still expensive,” Jump’s Ishan Bhatt wrote in an Oct. 16 review.
Engineers still had to reproduce reported problems and check whether the proposed attacks could work. Some submissions flagged apparent weaknesses while missing protections elsewhere in the software.
The backlog peaked at 299 open reports. As reviews slowed, other researchers rediscovered bugs that had already been submitted but remained unfixed or undisclosed. About 80% of duplicates arrived more than three days after the original report.
The competition had already charged $100 per submission and limited researchers to one report a day. Jump says charging discourages researchers from submitting large numbers of speculative findings and leaving its engineers to validate them.
Its new platform also limits each main report section to 3,000 characters.
The competition uncovered serious vulnerabilities, including a scheduling error that could make Firedancer execute transactions in the wrong order and disagree with other Solana validators about the resulting network state.
Meanwhile, Jump is increasing rewards alongside the submission cost. Eligible findings receive twice the standard payout through Nov. 20, or three times for bugs specific to Alpenglow, Solana’s new voting system. Critical Alpenglow findings can qualify for up to $300,000.

text:

US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) returned to net inflows on Monday despite weakening market sentiment and continued volatility in BTC price.
The funds attracted $110 million in net inflows on Monday, bouncing back from $774 million in withdrawals over the previous two trading sessions, according to SoSoValue.
Despite the rebound, October remained negative, with approximately $202 million in net outflows through Monday.

Market sentiment also weakened, with the Crypto Fear & Greed Index falling to 48 from 50 the previous day, while remaining in “Neutral” territory.
CryptoQuant data also showed retail investors sending more Bitcoin to Binance while large holders reduced their deposits.

title: Binance Files for Brazil Crypto License Ahead of Deadline
text:
The exchange is delisting 22 crypto assets for Brazilian users and hopes talks with the central bank will allow it to restore some services.
Binance has applied for a cryptocurrency service provider license in Brazil, seeking to maintain its operations in one of Latin America’s largest crypto markets ahead of a regulatory deadline on Friday, Oct. 30.
The exchange submitted its application to the Central Bank of Brazil on Friday, Oct. 23, through its local entity, BBrasil, according to a statement shared with Cointelegraph.
The company said the filing would allow Brazilian users to continue accessing crypto assets, stablecoin trading, payments and investment services.
Binance has also announced changes for Brazilian users effective Tuesday, including restrictions on crypto lending, margin trading and other services. The exchange is also delisting 22 crypto assets in the country.
“We support a regulated market that considers the characteristics of virtual assets, so that access to technology and innovation continues to advance, but we hope that the ongoing dialogue with the Central Bank will allow us to offer, in the near future, other products that were discontinued to comply with current regulations,” said Thiago Sarandy, Binance’s general manager in the country.
Brazil requires existing crypto service providers to submit authorization applications by Oct. 30 to continue operating under transitional arrangements. Filing an application does not constitute regulatory approval.

title: Lenders are done financing AI on faith, JPMorgan says
text:
An AI label alone doesn't secure funding as lenders now weigh a firm’s business and financial viability, according to JPMorgan.
“The AI label alone is no longer enough to reassure lenders. Companies must show that they can finance investment, service their debt and eventually turn spending into cash flow,” Justin Biemann, global investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, said in a report published Oct. 23.
Elon Musk issued a similar warning on Sunday, saying debt funding is drying up for AI neoclouds, firms whose revenue depends almost entirely on data centers.
That matters for crypto. AI has been one of the most potent narratives driving risk-taking across financial markets, bitcoin included. Bitcoin and Nvidia both bottomed within weeks of ChatGPT’s debut in late 2022 and have rallied significantly since. Instability in AI could therefore spill over into crypto.
These warnings come as markets grow uneasy over whether AI’s promise will show up on balance sheets. The tech-heavy Nasdaq has slid 6.7% to 29,263 from 31,360 since Oct. 6, with AI-linked firms such as Nvidia and Oracle falling more than the index.
The stress is showing up in credit markets too. The cost of insuring against defaults on the debt of several AI-linked firms has hit record levels. This insurance is called a credit default swap (CDS). The buyer pays a yearly premium, and if the borrower goes bankrupt or fails to pay, the buyer gets a large payout. The premium, also known as the spread, is quoted in basis points. At 100 basis points, insuring $10 million of debt costs $100,000 a year. A wider spread means investors want more compensation to take on the credit risk.
The scramble for CDS shows in volumes too. According to Morgan Stanley, weekly trading in CDS linked to bonds issued by Oracle (ORCL), SpaceX, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta META, Broadcom and Nvidia NVDA averaged more than $9 billion in September, up significantly from under $2 billion a week in July.
The picture is particularly worrying for the most debt-dependent firms. Without naming it, Biemann said one financing-dependent AI infrastructure company has taken on tens of billions of dollars in debt and other obligations. Its five-year CDS jumped to 1,100 basis points, so insuring $10 million of its debt would cost more than $1 million a year.
“Pricing at these levels implies near or above a 50% probability of default over five years, up from below 30% a year ago,” Biemann wrote.
Biemann pointed to Lehman Brothers as an example of CDS working as an early warning. Lehman’s CDS averaged less than 100 basis points in the third quarter of 2007 and topped 1,400 by mid-September 2008, when it filed for bankruptcy and rocked global markets.
Biemann said investors can view CDS today “as warning lights rather than countdown clocks.”
In other words, AI firms aren’t necessarily headed the Lehman way. Besides, activity in CDS tied to the large AI leaders looks more like hedging than positioning for a crisis.
Large AI leaders with strong cash flow pay 50 to 120 basis points for five-year protection, Biemann said. He said these levels “still look more like the price of portfolio insurance than a prediction of financial distress.”
Some established infrastructure borrowers have climbed toward 300 basis points. Protection on the broad investment grade market remains comparatively contained. “The concern is confined to business models that require debt markets to remain open while spending stays high and cash flow remains limited,” he said.

title: Bloom Bot Hackers Loot $953K Faster than You Can Microwave Popcorn
text:
Bloom pledged to reimburse nine traders after $953,000 was drained from 48 wallets, saying no private keys were accessed or compromised.
Hackers stole nearly $1 million from wallets linked to Telegram trading bot Bloom in under two minutes, according to blockchain analytics company Bitquery.
The attack drained $953,000 in 94 seconds from 48 cryptocurrency wallets belonging to nine traders who had used the bot, Bitquery reported Monday.
Bitquery said each drain was a Solana (SOL) transfer signed with the affected wallet’s private key.
Bloom pledged to reimburse all affected traders in full. In a later Monday statement, it attributed the attack to a remote code execution vulnerability in a third-party module and said no private keys had been accessed or compromised.
Trading bots such as Bloom hold users’ private keys to trade on their behalf, which can leave lingering security risks even after traders stop using them. Five wallets drained in the Bloom attack had been inactive on the bot since the first half of 2025, Bitquery said.
This is not the first time Telegram trading bot users have lost funds in an attack. In September 2024, Banana Gun reported that 11 users lost about $3 million. In October 2023, users of Telegram trading bots Maestro and Unibot lost a combined $1.1 million to exploits of their router contracts.

title: Now is the time to accumulate bitcoin, Galaxy says
text:
Bitcoin’s BTC$84.459,46 rally has stalled in recent weeks, leaving prices listless around $80,000. In a market where sentiment shifts quickly, this has led some bears to warn of a renewed price crash.
But Galaxy remains confident in bitcoin’s long-term prospects, saying it’s time to accumulate.
“We think the bear market ended in June and that bitcoin is in the accumulation phase that has preceded every prior advance,” Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, said in a note titled “Why now is the time to add and hold BTC.”
Galaxy Digital is a U.S. financial and infrastructure firm founded in 2018 by billionaire Mike Novogratz. It is headquartered in New York City and trades on Nasdaq under the ticker GLXY.
According to Thorn, the bear market likely ended in June under $58,000, and improving price-chart signals, reduced selling pressure, and mounting fiscal risks make the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization attractive to accumulate.
He added that bitcoin has entered an accumulation phase resembling periods that preceded previous advances.

title: Ripple Wins Final OCC Approval for Trust Bank Behind $2.6B RLUSD Stablecoin - Decrypt
text:
Ripple has received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to establish Ripple National Trust Bank, a federally supervised national trust bank, the company said on Monday.
The approval completes a process that began when the OCC conditionally approved Ripple's application in December 2025, alongside those of Circle, Paxos, Fidelity Digital Assets and BitGo.
Once open, the bank will manage the segregated reserves backing the Ripple USD (RLUSD) stablecoin, act as collateral trustee of those reserves for the benefit of RLUSD holders, and provide fiduciary digital asset custody services to enterprises. RLUSD will still be issued by Standard Custody & Trust Company, Ripple's limited purpose trust company regulated by the New York Department of Financial Services, so the stablecoin will now sit under both state and federal supervision.
"For years, we've said crypto and banks work better together. Final approval for Ripple National Trust Bank is what that looks like in practice," Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse said in the release. In a tweet, he added: "The revolution isn't happening outside the system. It's happening from within it."
Big news heading into @RippleSwell: the @USOCC has granted final approval for Ripple National Trust Bank.
This gives Ripple a federally supervised platform to support $RLUSD and provide digital asset custody to enterprises.
We’ve always said crypto and banks work better…
— Brad Garlinghouse (@bgarlinghouse) October 26, 2026
Launched in December 2024, RLUSD has a market capitalization of about $2.6 billion, according to CoinGecko. Ripple says the stablecoin is used across its payments network and as collateral within its Ripple Prime brokerage. BNY is the stablecoin's primary reserve custodian.
XRP, the cryptocurrency closely associated with Ripple, rose 0.5% over the past 24 hours to $1.29, according to CoinGecko, one of only two top-10 coins by market cap to gain on the day alongside Zcash.
The national trust charters the OCC has handed to crypto firms remain contested. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) has argued, in a letter to Comptroller Jonathan Gould, that the approvals for firms including Coinbase and Ripple violated the National Bank Act. "These companies are effectively crypto banks that want to evade the fundamental safeguards and obligations that come with being a bank," she wrote.
The Digital Chamber, a crypto industry trade group, urged the OCC to "defend these charter approvals and continue developing clear supervisory expectations for trust banks."
Earlier this month, the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC in federal court, arguing that the charters have become "a side door into the banking system for crypto firms" that avoid the capital requirements, consolidated supervision and FDIC insurance that bind traditional banks.
Ripple said it will keep working with the OCC, NYDFS and other regulators as the bank begins operations and as the U.S. implements the GENIUS Act's stablecoin framework.

title: Crypto wallet maker Keystone is destroying nearly 19,000 devices after a major security breach
text:
Hardware wallet maker Keystone said it will destroy almost 19,000 unsold devices and suspend shipments after a website breach exposed customer information and a key that could let counterfeit wallets pass authenticity checks.
An attacker gained access to the company’s website on Oct. 20 through a flaw in a third-party data monitoring tool, Keystone said Monday in a post on X. The attack exposed 25,964 buyer records from 2024 through 2026, including names, contact details, shipping addresses and order information. Another 12,873 unpaid checkout records may have been affected.
The breach adds to a string of attacks on hardware wallet users this year. At Ledger, criminals fitted devices sold through resellers in Southeast Asia, with hidden components capturing recovery phrases during setup. Similarly, a flaw in Coldcard’s seed-generation software let attackers reconstruct private keys and drain wallets remotely.
The stolen Keystone key is built into devices during production and cannot be changed. It allows wallets to pass online authenticity checks, raising the risk that fake devices could appear genuine and put users' funds at risk, according to the firm. The company said it will destroy 18,835 unsold units.
Keystone said the breach did not expose recovery phrases, private keys or wallet credentials.
Some customer records should have been deleted under Keystone's 180-day retention policy, but an automated deletion tool failed without the company detecting the issue, it said.
“We failed to fulfill our commitment to erase customer data on time, and we accept responsibility for this failure,” Keystone wrote.
Keystone’s update came a day after hardware wallet maker Foundation disclosed a separate breach in which attackers sent phishing emails that appeared to come from its official domains.
Foundation said it had identified more than 23,000 phishing email attempts. It found no evidence that Passport devices or private keys were compromised.
Foundation also found older database copies that its 60-day data deletion process had missed. In an update, it said attackers could access records containing about 5,600 mailing addresses and 5,200 phone numbers, though it could not confirm how many were accessed.
Keystone said devices delivered before Oct. 20 remain safe to use if they pass authentication, while customers who received devices using the old key after that date should seek further checks before use.
The company said users do not need to move funds due to the breach alone and warned against fake recall or asset migration messages.
Keystone will replace the authentication key in new devices, shift website sales to preorders and cut customer data retention to 90 days, it added.

title: Japan's top yen stablecoin falls short of its target in a disappointing first year
text:
Japan's JPYC stablecoin has fallen well short of expectations in its first year, reaching just a quarter of its issuer's circulation target despite a string of corporate partnerships.
“Frankly, I don’t think it’s growing,” CEO Noritaka Okabe told NADA NEWS in an interview, acknowledging that the yen-backed token had failed to gain the traction the company expected. He said trading volume was “not bad,” but wasn’t satisfied with the amount in circulation.
Only 3.2 billion yen (around $20 million) was in circulation as of Oct. 23, compared with cumulative issuance of 12.1 billion yen, Nikkei reported. That data is near the $20.85 million DeFiLlama shows, and reflects tokens that have since been redeemed, underscoring the challenge of keeping JPYC in circulation.
Circulation briefly topped 4.2 billion yen in September after South Korean exchange Upbit listed JPYC. The listing pushed its market price above 1 yen and sent traders rushing to mint new tokens for arbitrage.
Okabe estimated that about 35 billion yen changed hands across Upbit and Uniswap in a single day, before circulation fell back to around 3 billion yen.
That matters for JPYC's business model as the stablecoin is backed by bank deposits and Japanese government bonds, with its issuer earning interest on those reserves. Less money in circulation means less potential interest income.
Okabe blamed the disappointing results in part on a 1 million yen daily issuance limit tied to Japan's Type II funds-transfer rules. JPYC eased its restrictions in May, allowing 1 million yen per request rather than per day, but still restricts rapid repeat transactions.
The cap has frustrated corporate adoption. Software company Asteria, which plans to hold 1 billion yen in JPYC, has been forced to build its balance through installments.
The weak results also contrast with JPYC's growing list of partners. Logistics firm AZ-COM Maruwa signed an alliance in July to develop payments for about 2,300 business partners.
SBJ Bank and LINE NEXT also agreed earlier this month to test bank-linked stablecoin wallet top-ups, though the project remains in the trial stage. Meanwhile, Japan's Financial Services Agency is reviewing stablecoin regulations, with a roadmap expected in early 2027.
Okabe now wants circulation to reach tens of billions of yen in JPYC's second year, a roughly tenfold increase from current levels.

title: Why This Team of Ninjas Is Tripling Down on Mining Bitcoin - Decrypt
text:
Ninjas in Pyjamas Group, the company behind the legendary esports team, has acquired a third batch of Bitcoin miners in exchange for over 247 million Class A ordinary shares.
Hicham Chahine, the founder and CEO of NIP Group, told Decrypt that he wants to bet on Bitcoin mining while the market is "cooling," rather than when it's hot and competition is higher. He added that the facilities could be used for artificial intelligence in the future.
"Now that this tranche is closed, we're at roughly 13.85 EH/s. That puts us among the largest publicly listed miners in the world, roughly 195 Bitcoin a month," Chahine said. "That's real revenue, and it supports everything else we're building. This year we reviewed every single piece of NIP Group, not just mining. We made decisions with one goal: better margins and a clear path to profitability. Mining had to earn its place in that review, and it did."
It comes after the esports team expanded its Bitcoin operation last year as it looked to mine 160 Bitcoin a month. This most recent acquisition brings that target up by 35 Bitcoin to 195 Bitcoin a month, or $2.8 million at today's prices.
Chahine told Decrypt that NIP Group is "optimistic about where this is heading," adding that the third batch of Bitcoin miners will require "minimal ramp time."
NIP Group is a digital entertainment company known for esports and gaming ventures. It owns Ninjas in Pyjamas, which fields professional esports teams in games like Counter-Strike 2, Valorant, League of Legends, and Rocket League.
The firm's stock, NIPG, has dropped 40.7% from $6.74 to $4 since the Bitcoin announcement last week, according to Yahoo Finance data. This marks an all-time low for the stock. Bitcoin has dropped 2% to $79,820 over the same period of time, per Decrypt data.
Chahine explained that the purchased facilities could shift to focus on artificial intelligence infrastructure if the market demands.
"We look at what AI and [high-performance computing] customers will actually pay, how long they'll commit and whether that demand is sustained or temporary," Chahine told Decrypt. "When those workloads clearly beat mining on returns, consistently and not just for a week or two, that's when we may move capacity. If the numbers say shift, we shift."
Of course, any sort of future pivot would require notable legwork, as Bitcoin miners can't simply be turned into AI data centers at the flick of a switch. But, Chahine said, the infrastructure around the mining facilities is a good foundation for what AI and high-performance computing need.
"When we talk about AI, we mean using that footprint and that know-how for compute-heavy work when the economics make sense," he said. "We're a gaming and entertainment company at heart, and our fans already live on compute, bringing infrastructure and entertainment under one roof makes sense."

title: Zcash co-founder proposes ending grants subsidy, citing $125 million treasury
text: Zcash co-founder Sean Bowe on Monday submitted a proposal seeking to end automatic funding for the Zcash Community Grants program and redirect its remaining 8% share of block subsidies to the network's Network Sustainability Mechanism. "It's time to turn off the ZCG funding stream," Bowe wrote on X. "ZCG has over $125M in funding, and will receive millions more before the spigot is turned off. Builders seeking funding can access it through open grants or invite-only grants, with approvals cleared by a five-person committee elected by the Zcash (ZEC) community. According to the draft proposal, ZCG holds 91,452.98 ZEC and approximately $8.8 million in U.S. dollar-denominated assets, against $2.4 million in outstanding grant liabilities. Bowe said the existing 8% allocation model can yield over $68 million in ZEC annually, way above the $1.53 million in ZCG expenses reported by the Financial Privacy Foundation for the first quarter of 2026. If approved, the proposal would redirect the allocation to the NSM for the remainder of the existing funding stream's term without increasing Zcash’s issued supply, per the draft. Meanwhile, a separate 12% allocation to the Coinholder-Controlled Fund would remain unchanged, Bowe said. ZCG would still retain control of its existing assets and could continue approving grants and meeting outstanding commitments, he added. The proposal has no assigned activation height and is not included in the currently specified NU7 network upgrade. It would require a future network upgrade to take effect. title: Analysis Sees New Bitcoin Bull Market as Older Coins’ Realized Cap Share Drops
text:
A decline in the share of Bitcoin’s realized cap held by coins unmoved for 18 months or longer points to the ‘early stages’ of a bull market, analysis says.
Bitcoin (BTC) onchain transaction data is hinting at the start of a new uptrend as long-term holders retreat from selling.
Data from onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant shows that investors holding coins for 18 months or longer are starting to become less active.
On Sept. 16, the 18-month-plus cohort’s share of realized cap — the value of all coins at the price they last moved onchain — hit 26.98%, its highest since mid-November 2024.
Analyzing the data, CryptoQuant sees a historical trend that preceded Bitcoin bull markets now repeating.

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.
Somebody bought a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal this weekend to tell public company CEOs that crypto is coming for their shares.
“YOUR STOCK. THEIR TOKENS. YOUR PROBLEM,” it read, paid for by the Common Sense Leadership Fund, a conservative nonprofit. They listed eight risks - pricing disparities, obscured ownership, impaired capital raising, cybertheft, market manipulation, AML and KYC loopholes, absent investor protections, legal liability. And the call to action was blunt: the SEC has given you the right to opt out, you have 30 days, this is your only chance.
The war against tokenized stocks is brewing.
Nine companies objected to having their shares tokenized on the OKX-ICE venue on October 15. By October 19 it was 16. By October 23, the list hit 22, including Wells Fargo, Cisco, Marvell, Arm, Moderna and Intuit joining Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Verizon, Broadcom and UnitedHealth. That’s a two-and-a-half-fold increase in eight days, and 35% of the 63 companies the venue planned to list.
OKXICE even amended its rules on October 19 to let issuers tokenize their own shares, which would hand them control. Not one objector has taken it. They don’t want a better version of the product. They don’t want it.
Robinhood reports third-quarter results after the bell, and no company has more riding on how this fight resolves.
Robinhood Chain launched its public mainnet on July 1. In its debut quarter it generated roughly $51 million in revenue. That’s more than Ethereum’s $41 million, while Ethereum’s own network revenue fell 35%. It processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth among all networks.
Of that, $13.7 billion was tokenized equities. One fifth of everything trading on the chain, in a single quarter, from a zero start.
Robinhood’s stock tokens have already drawn fire (AMC’s CEO called them “contemptible”) and the company is building an entire ecosystem on top of them. Long.xyz pairs memecoins against tokenized NVDA and TSLA, and meme-versus-stock pairs now drive most stock-token volume on the chain. Orbio funds AI inference credits with creator fees paid in tokenized NVDA. Pull the stock tokens out, and a lot of that architecture has nothing to stand on.
So will Vlad Tenev address the tokenized stock war? It’s the billion-dollar question. A tweet from Monday makes it seem like perhaps he will. We will find out soon enough...

title: Luxor Technology raises $16M to expand AI hardware brokerage and compute trading
text:
Bitcoin mining companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI), renting out computing power and converting mining facilities into data centers. Now, some of the companies that built their businesses serving bitcoin miners are following them into the AI market.
Luxor Technology, best known for its bitcoin mining services, is also moving into AI hardware and trading contracts that allow companies to agree on computing prices in advance.
The Seattle-based company said on Tuesday that it raised $16 million in a round led by CMT Digital. Bitcoin mining equipment makers Canaan and MicroBT also invested. Luxor said the money will go toward its AI hardware brokerage and computing-power trading business.
The round included new investment and sales of existing shares, although Luxor did not disclose how much of the new funding was invested in the company.
Publicly traded bitcoin miners had signed more than $70 billion worth of AI and high-performance computing contracts by the end of March, according to CoinShares data.
Not everyone is moving away from bitcoin mining. Nasdaq-listed NIP Group (NIPG) announced plans last week to essentially increase its mining capacity by about 48%. The company said it expects to generate about 195 bitcoin a month at full deployment.
Moving into AI also requires more than access to electricity. Ethan Vera, Luxor's chief operating officer, told CoinDesk that its software business works with bitcoin miners representing nearly two gigawatts of power capacity.
After assessing more than half that capacity, Luxor found that most sites had sufficient electricity and fiber connections for AI workloads but would require new data centers.
Luxor is also expanding into contracts that allow buyers and sellers to agree on future computing prices, much as bitcoin miners use financial contracts to manage changes in mining revenue.
Sam Hallene, a partner at CMT Digital, said AI companies have different reasons to protect themselves against price changes, including the possibility that expensive computing equipment remains useful longer than expected.
"We don’t know exactly what the market structure will look like at the end of the day," Hallene told CoinDesk.
Luxor already offers privately negotiated contracts tied to computing rental prices, although the market is still developing. Vera said transparency remains a problem, particularly around AI hardware prices.
In August, Luxor introduced a price index that tracks daily asking prices for Nvidia AI server systems, providing buyers and sellers with a reference point for equipment prices.

title: Crypto Could Outperform AI Stocks: Wall Street’s Jordi Visser
text:
Former Morgan Stanley and Weiss executive Jordi Visser says AI agents are boosting demand for crypto as he expands his holdings beyond Bitcoin, Ether and Solana.
Cryptocurrencies could deliver a better payoff from the artificial intelligence boom than AI stocks themselves, according to Visser Labs founder Jordi Visser.
Explosive gains in AI stocks are becoming harder to repeat, Visser tells Cointelegraph’s Trade Secrets. At the same time, AI agents are creating demand for crypto payments and tokenized assets.
“Without AI, I don’t think crypto would be going through this bull market,” he says.
Hyperscaler capital spending and free cash flow (left), and forward valuations compared with the S&P 500 (right). Source: JPMorgan Asset Management
As a result of his thesis, he has expanded his own holdings beyond Bitcoin, Ether and Solana into a broader basket of tokens.
Visser’s three-decade career includes stints as managing director at Morgan Stanley and chief investment officer at Weiss Multi-Strategy Advisers. He now heads 22V’s AI Macro Nexus Research.
The Wall Street veteran’s broader bet is that AI agents will allow people to instruct software to execute trades and other financial transactions on their behalf.
“AI agents are effectively the same as the App Store or the smartphone for crypto,” he says.
In that scenario, users would direct their agents while the software handles execution. The growing use of those agents will drive more activity in tokenized assets and crypto payments, extending the investment opportunity beyond the companies supplying computing power.
Related: AI potential to drive crypto demand remains ‘underappreciated’: BlackRock
But Visser’s crypto outlook still carries exposure to the AI trade he has grown more cautious about. He identifies a severe AI downturn that drags down equity markets as one threat to his bullish case.
“I don’t think that would end the bull market, but I definitely think it would retest the lows that we just saw,” he says.
Visser says he began reducing his exposure to memory chipmaker Micron in mid-May after concluding that hedge funds and retail investors had crowded into the AI trade.
“One of the reasons that Bitcoin and Ethereum were having such a hard time is because the focus was completely on AI,” he says.
By mid-May, Bitcoin was down 10.85% for the year and Ether about 25.86%. Source: TradingView
AI offered investors potentially greener pastures backed by rising business revenue. Microsoft’s quarterly report on April 29 claimed that its AI business was generating revenue at an annualized rate of $37 billion, more than double a year earlier. Meanwhile, Micron reported in March that its fiscal second-quarter revenue had nearly tripled to $23.86 billion.
But AI investors now face a less forgiving market, according to Visser. The 100-stock AI portfolio he tracks is up about 40% this year, but has become more volatile than Bitcoin on a rolling 126-day measure.
Related: Agents can trade 24/7 — but Yat Siu warns you could lose access at any time
Financing concerns have since hit AI infrastructure, as building them costs more than companies generate from their existing businesses at present.
For example, Oracle spent $55.7 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026 against $32 billion in operating cash flow, and raised $43 billion in debt financing.
“I didn’t say AI was over. AI fireworks show is over,” Visser says.
He still sees several years of growth ahead in computing demand from AI agents, but says investors should temper their expectations for stock returns.
Until August, Visser’s crypto holdings consisted solely of Bitcoin, Ether and Solana. While Bitcoin remains his largest position, he has since started to acquire a broader range of tokens.
Dogecoin is a clear signal he watches for returning retail enthusiasm, which he considers essential to sustaining a broader rally.
“They’re the energy of the space and they’re the ones that are going to fuel this as other people get involved,” he says.
To track that broader market, Visser maintains an equally weighted index of 42 tokens and four publicly traded stocks. He says it has outperformed Bitcoin since June and plans to hold all its constituents.
Privacy is a theme he has already invested in.
“I’m not betting on one company, but I believe in privacy,” Visser says.
He says AI will make privacy and identity protection more important as fraud and other forms of abuse grow. Zcash and Monero among projects that fit that investment thesis.

title: Polymarket Has Investigated 'Dozens' of Midterm Election Bets: Report - Decrypt
text:
Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its midterm election markets for possible insider trading and manipulation, the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista, told NPR.
At least two of those investigations have been referred to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, NPR reported, citing a person familiar with the probes.
Bautista, a former FBI official and crypto analyst who joined Polymarket in June, said her team of 16 is policing election bets with a new surveillance system ahead of the November 3 vote.
"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," she said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."
Her team monitors both Polymarket's U.S.-regulated exchange, which requires users to verify their identities, and Polymarket International, where users can trade anonymously with crypto. Even so, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely fully anonymous. "There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," she said.
The system pulls in data from social media, Federal Election Commission filings, crypto companies, banking partners and statistical models, and alerts Bautista when a user trips enough internal red flags. "We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," she said. She declined to share the specific criteria, citing system security.
Election markets are especially vulnerable, Barnard College economics professor Rajiv Sethi told NPR, because they "have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," with perceptions of a candidate's momentum able to influence the result.
Kalshi, Polymarket's main rival, launched its own FEC-based system in May to block campaign staffers from betting on elections. In June, it added employment disclosures for high-risk markets and a risk-scoring framework, saying it had opened more than 150 investigations that year and referred more than 20 cases to law enforcement. One campaign staffer told NPR they had found a way around Kalshi's block.
Election insider trading drew scrutiny in May, when campaign staffers told NPR they had made "thousands" betting on their own candidates using tips about unreleased polls. "Because you have all this information and knowledge that isn't publicly available yet, it's almost foolish not to bet on it before it's made public," one said. Jeff Le Riche, a former CFTC trial lawyer, told the outlet that such trades "could potentially be a violation" of the law.
Polymarket partnered with blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis on market surveillance tools in April, days after an active-duty U.S. Army soldier was charged with using classified information about the raid to capture Nicolás Maduro to bet on Polymarket. The soldier, who has pleaded not guilty, allegedly placed more than $33,000 in bets and won nearly $410,000. Polymarket said it detected the activity and reported it to authorities before the arrest.
NPR reported that the CFTC has done little to police prediction markets, largely leaving the work to the companies. In September, though, CFTC staff warned that "mention markets," contracts on whether a named person says certain words or attends an event, should be presumed readily susceptible to manipulation. The advisory came three weeks after the agency fined a teleprompter operator who traded on speeches he had already read.

title: CF Benchmarks brings Wall Street pricing infrastructure onchain, including data used by BlackRock
text:
CF Benchmarks, whose pricing indices underpin BlackRock's bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) and CME Group's crypto futures, is bringing its market data to blockchain networks as more financial firms look to offer traditional investment products through decentralized finance (DeFi).
The company, which is owned by Kraken parent Payward, has introduced CFB Oracle, a service that gives blockchain applications access to its benchmarks for cryptocurrencies, stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies.
The idea is to make the same pricing infrastructure used by major financial institutions available to developers building investment products on blockchains.
For example, a blockchain-based fund holding tokenized stocks would need reliable prices to calculate the value of its portfolio. A lending platform accepting tokenized bonds as collateral would need that data to determine how much users can borrow and when positions should be liquidated.
CF Benchmarks already provides this type of pricing data to traditional financial markets. Its indices are used by products representing more than $120 billion in assets, according to the company.
With CFB Oracle, developers can use those benchmarks to build products such as onchain index funds, tokenized portfolios and derivatives without having to develop their own pricing systems. The service is available on Ethereum ETH$2,490.55, HyperEVM and Robinhood Chain, with plans to support other compatible networks.
CF Benchmarks says the data is digitally signed, allowing applications to check that prices came from the company and haven't been altered. It also publishes each index at the same frequency for all customers, rather than charging for faster access.
The service has a planned use within Payward. The Kraken parent intends to use CFB Oracle to supply pricing data for an upcoming U.S. perpetual futures offering powered by Hyperliquid (HYPE). That product is still awaiting regulatory approval.
The launch puts CF Benchmarks in competition with oracle providers such as Chainlink LINK$12.64 and Pyth, which already supply market data to decentralized trading and lending platforms.
CFB Oracle won't issue funds or handle trades itself. Its role is to supply the reference prices those products need to operate.

title: Crypto Market Structure Explained: Liquidity & Venues | The Block
text: Crypto market structure describes the systems, venues, participants, incentives, and rules that determine how digital assets are traded. It includes exchanges, order books, automated market makers, liquidity providers, derivatives venues, custodians, market makers, institutional investors, fundraising mechanisms, venture capital, arbitrage, and MEV. This intermediate guide assumes familiarity with digital assets, exchanges, wallets, tokens, DeFi fundamentals, and blockchain transactions. What you’ll learn Crypto market structure examines how markets work behind the scenes. The focus is market mechanics rather than trading strategy: how systems and participants shape liquidity, price discovery, execution quality, institutional access, fundraising, arbitrage, and MEV. Foundations of crypto market structure; Centralized and decentralized trading venues; Order types, matching, spread, slippage, and execution quality; Derivatives, perpetual futures, funding rates, leverage, and liquidations; Market participants, infrastructure, custodians, prime brokers, and market makers; Market indicators such as volume, market cap, FDV, open interest, funding rates, RSI, and moving averages; Institutional investors, ETFs, OTC desks, custody, and execution algorithms; Fundraising mechanisms, tokenomics, vesting, unlocks, and regulatory constraints; Crypto venture capital and how token liquidity changes incentives; Arbitrage, MEV, private order flow, sandwich attacks, and execution fairness. Learning outcomes Explain how crypto market structure shapes liquidity, price discovery, and execution outcomes; Connect order types, spread, slippage, leverage, funding, and liquidations to real market outcomes; Identify major market participants and explain how their incentives shape market dynamics; Interpret indicators within the context of underlying market structure rather than using them as standalone predictions; Evaluate arbitrage and MEV dynamics and explain how they affect efficiency, fairness, and user costs. Course lesson summaries The lesson summaries below are a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Market Structure 201 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities. Lesson 1 – Foundations of Market Structure Defines market structure through its participants, venues, mechanisms, and rules and connects CEXs, DEXs, order books, AMMs, custody, clearing, and settlement to liquidity, price discovery, and execution quality. Lesson 2 – Order Types & Execution Compares market, limit, stop, IOC, FOK, GTC, and iceberg orders and follows how spread, depth, matching, fill priority, and slippage affect execution. Lesson 3 – Derivatives & Structured Products Introduces futures, options, and perpetuals, then connects leverage, funding, and liquidation cascades with structured products such as covered-call and delta-neutral vaults. Lesson 4 – Market Participants & Infrastructure Maps retail traders, institutions, market makers, HFT firms, validators, miners, custodians, prime brokers, data providers, and settlement systems across the market ecosystem. Lesson 5 – Market Indicators Covers volume, market cap, FDV, spread, depth, open interest, funding rates, RSI, moving averages, and sentiment while emphasizing that signals need context. Lesson 6 – Institutional Investors Shows how hedge funds, asset managers, treasuries, prop shops, banks, and brokers use custody, OTC desks, ETFs, prime brokers, and execution algorithms to enter crypto markets. Lesson 7 – Fundraising Mechanisms Compares ICOs, IEOs, IDOs, STOs, SPVs, syndicates, launch platforms, and DAO fundraising and considers how regulation, tokenomics, vesting, and unlocks shape incentives. Lesson 8 – Venture Capital in Crypto Examines how token liquidity changes investment timelines, governance influence, and incentives, including the trade-off between concentrated capital and decentralization. Lesson 9 – Arbitrage & MEV Connects spatial, triangular, and statistical arbitrage across fragmented venues with transaction ordering, sandwich attacks, backrunning, private order flow, and flash loans. Market structure at a glance Participants: These include those who trade, provide liquidity, validate, custody, fund, or build infrastructure. Different participants have different incentives and constraints. Venues: Trading takes place across CEXs, DEXs, OTC desks, and derivatives platforms. Venue design shapes execution, custody, transparency, and risk. Liquidity: This describes how easily assets can be bought or sold without major price impact. Liquidity affects spreads, slippage, volatility, and execution quality. Price discovery: This is how markets convert information and order flow into prices. Fragmented venues can create price differences and arbitrage opportunities. Derivatives: These contracts reshape exposure without requiring ownership of the underlying asset. Leverage, funding, and liquidations can amplify market moves. Infrastructure: This includes custody, prime brokerage, settlement, market data, routing, validators, and middleware. Infrastructure determines access, reliability, and institutional readiness. What is crypto market structure? Market structure is the architecture of a market: the participants, venues, mechanisms, and rules that support trading. In crypto, this includes centralized exchanges, decentralized exchanges, order books, AMMs, custody models, settlement systems, market makers, institutional execution channels, and blockchain-specific dynamics such as MEV. A market can have high volume and still have poor execution quality if liquidity is shallow, fragmented, or concentrated. A market can also appear decentralized at the asset layer while depending on centralized venues, custodians, or data providers. Market-structure analysis reveals those hidden dependencies. Trading venues: CEXs, DEXs, and OTC desks Crypto trading happens across many venues. Centralized exchanges custody user assets, run internal matching engines, and update balances on internal ledgers. Decentralized exchanges let users trade through smart contracts while retaining custody. OTC desks help large participants execute bigger trades without showing full order flow on public books. Each venue model makes different trade-offs. CEXs can offer speed, customer support, and deep order books, but they introduce custody and counterparty risk. DEXs offer transparency and self-custody, but users face smart contract risk, slippage, MEV, and on-chain transaction costs. OTC trading can reduce visible market impact for large orders, but it depends on trusted counterparties and institutional relationships. Comparing trading venues Centralized exchanges (CEXs) offer fast matching, familiar user experiences, deep liquidity, and fiat access. Their trade-offs include custody risk, opaque internal ledgers, and regulatory exposure. Decentralized exchanges (DEXs) offer self-custody, transparency, and smart-contract settlement. Their trade-offs include smart contract risk, slippage, MEV, and on-chain transaction costs. Over-the-counter (OTC) desks support large-block execution with reduced visible market impact. However, they depend on counterparties and generally offer less public transparency. Order types, spread, and slippage Order types encode trader priorities. A market order prioritizes immediate execution. A limit order prioritizes price control. Stop orders, IOC, FOK, GTC, and iceberg orders add more specific execution instructions. These orders interact with order books, matching engines, spreads, depth, and venue risk checks. After an order enters a venue, it passes the venue's risk controls, joins or crosses the order book, receives priority under the matching rules, and may fill fully, partially, or not at all. The instruction determines how long it can remain active and whether an incomplete fill is acceptable. Spread is the gap between the best available buy and sell prices. Slippage is the difference between expected and executed price. Both are part of execution cost. They become especially important in fast markets, thin markets, or fragmented markets where liquidity is spread across venues. Liquidity and price discovery Liquidity is the ease with which an asset can be bought or sold without significantly moving the price. Price discovery is the process by which markets convert information, order flow, and trading activity into asset prices. In crypto, price discovery can be fragmented because the same asset may trade on multiple exchanges, DEX pools, derivatives venues, and OTC channels. Market makers and liquidity providers help reduce spreads and support smoother execution by continuously quoting prices or supplying assets to pools. Their participation improves market quality, but it also depends on incentives, risk limits, volatility, and access to reliable infrastructure. Derivatives, perpetual futures, and funding rates Derivatives are instruments that reshape exposure without requiring ownership of the underlying asset. In crypto, perpetual futures are especially important. They have no expiry date and use funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with the spot market. Funding rates are recurring payments between long and short traders. When perpetual prices trade above spot, longs usually pay shorts. When perpetual prices trade below spot, shorts may pay longs. Funding rates can signal positioning pressure, but they should not be read as standalone predictions. Other derivatives include dated futures and options, while structured products combine instruments into packaged risk-and-return profiles. Covered-call vaults exchange some upside for option premium, and delta-neutral vaults try to reduce directional exposure by combining offsetting positions. Their apparent yield still depends on leverage, volatility, collateral, and execution risk. Key derivatives concepts Perpetual futures: Derivatives with no expiry that track spot prices through funding payments. They are a major source of leverage and positioning data. Funding rate: A recurring payment between long and short perpetual futures traders. It helps align perpetual and spot prices and can indicate crowded positioning. Open interest: The total number of open contracts. It provides information about outstanding leverage and market participation. Liquidation: The forced closing of a leveraged position when margin is insufficient. Liquidations can amplify volatility and create cascading market moves. Market participants and infrastructure Crypto markets include retail traders, institutional investors, hedge funds, asset managers, corporate treasuries, market makers, high-frequency trading firms, custodians, prime brokers, OTC desks, data providers, validators, miners, and protocol teams. Each participant interacts with the market through different constraints and incentives. Institutions usually need custody, compliance, execution quality, reporting, and risk controls before they can participate at scale. This is why infrastructure matters. Custodians, prime brokers, market data providers, settlement systems, and execution algorithms shape how institutional capital enters and moves through crypto markets. Market indicators: useful, but context-dependent Market indicators translate activity into signals, but they do not explain markets on their own. Volume, market cap, FDV, open interest, funding rates, RSI, moving averages, spread, depth, and sentiment measures are useful only when interpreted in context. For example, rising open interest can mean more participation, but it can also mean more leverage. A high funding rate can signal strong long demand, but it can also suggest crowded positioning. The aim is to read these indicators as part of a system rather than as automatic predictions. Institutional investors, ETFs, and treasury vehicles Institutional participation changes market structure because large investors need reliable custody, liquidity, reporting, compliance, and execution workflows. Hedge funds, asset managers, banks, brokers, corporate treasuries, and prop shops may all interact with crypto differently. ETFs, OTC desks, prime brokers, execution algorithms, and custody providers can make digital asset exposure easier for institutions to access. They can also change flows, liquidity concentration, and market behavior. Digital asset treasury companies and related vehicles introduce another layer of market structure by linking corporate balance sheets, token exposure, premiums, discounts, and investor demand. Execution algorithms such as TWAP and VWAP can divide large orders across time or observed market volume to reduce visible impact. They do not eliminate execution risk, especially when liquidity is fragmented or volatility rises. Fundraising, tokenomics, and crypto venture capital Crypto fundraising can happen through equity, tokens, or hybrid structures. ICOs, IEOs, IDOs, STOs, SPVs, syndicates, launch platforms, and DAO fundraising each shape incentives differently. Tokenomics, vesting, unlock schedules, circulating supply, and governance rights can all affect market behavior after launch. Crypto venture capital also differs from traditional venture capital because tokens can create earlier liquidity, different governance influence, and new incentive conflicts. Capital concentration may help projects launch and scale, but it can also create decentralization and market-pressure trade-offs. Arbitrage and MEV Arbitrage happens when participants act on temporary price differences across venues or instruments. In fragmented crypto markets, spatial, triangular, and statistical arbitrage can help prices converge. This can improve efficiency, but it can also favor participants with better infrastructure, faster routing, or more capital. MEV, or maximal extractable value, is value captured through transaction inclusion, exclusion, or ordering. It can appear through sandwich attacks, backrunning, private order flow, and flash-loan-enabled strategies. MEV is a market-structure issue because it connects trading, execution, blockchain ordering, user experience, and fairness. Risks and misconceptions High trading volume does not guarantee strong liquidity or fair execution. Liquidity can disappear quickly during volatility. Funding rates and open interest are context signals, not price predictions. Leverage can amplify both gains and losses and can contribute to liquidation cascades. CEXs, DEXs, and OTC desks each introduce different risks rather than one model being universally safer. MEV and arbitrage are not just advanced trading topics; they affect execution quality and user costs. This page explains market mechanics and does not provide trading, investment, tax, or legal advice. Key takeaways Crypto market structure explains how digital asset markets are organized and how they function behind the scenes. Liquidity, price discovery, execution quality, and fairness depend on venues, participants, infrastructure, and incentives. CEXs, DEXs, and OTC desks each solve different market needs and introduce different risks. Derivatives, perpetual futures, funding rates, open interest, leverage, and liquidations can strongly affect market behavior. Institutional investors need custody, compliance, reporting, and execution infrastructure before participating at scale. Fundraising models, tokenomics, vesting, unlocks, and VC incentives can shape market dynamics after launch. Arbitrage can improve price efficiency, while MEV can create hidden costs and fairness trade-offs. Market indicators are useful only when interpreted in the context of underlying market structure. Before you start This is an intermediate topic. Helpful background knowledge includes digital asset basics, exchanges, wallets, tokens, DeFi fundamentals, and basic blockchain transaction flow. Continue learning Related topics include DeFi 201, Ethereum & Layer 1s 201, Scaling & Layer 2s 201, Bitcoin 201, and advanced modules on institutional infrastructure, regulation, stablecoins, and risk management. Glossary Market structure: The systems, rules, participants, venues, and incentives that govern how assets are traded. Price discovery: The process by which markets convert information and trading activity into asset prices. Liquidity: The ease with which an asset can be bought or sold without major price impact. CEX: A centralized exchange that custodies assets, matches orders internally, and updates balances on internal ledgers. DEX: A decentralized exchange where users trade through smart contracts while retaining custody. Order book: A venue mechanism that organizes buy and sell orders by price and time priority. Spread: The gap between the best available buy and sell prices. Slippage: The difference between expected and executed trade price. Perpetual futures: Crypto derivatives with no expiration that use funding payments to stay aligned with spot prices. Funding rate: A recurring payment between long and short perpetual futures traders. Open interest: The total number of open futures or perpetual contracts. Liquidation: Forced closing of a leveraged position when margin falls below required levels. Market maker: A participant that continuously quotes buy and sell prices to provide liquidity. Prime broker: An institutional service provider offering margin, execution, liquidity access, and consolidated reporting. FDV: Fully diluted valuation; the value of all tokens if the maximum supply were circulating. Tokenomics: The supply, emissions, vesting, utility, and incentive design of a token system. Crypto VC: Venture capital investing in crypto projects, often through equity, tokens, or hybrid structures. Arbitrage: Acting on temporary price differences across venues or instruments. MEV: Maximal extractable value; value captured by controlling transaction inclusion, exclusion, or ordering. Sandwich attack: An MEV strategy that places trades before and after a user swap to capture slippage. Flash loan: A loan that must be borrowed and repaid within a single transaction, often used in arbitrage.
